A Friday Vanity Fair exclusive painted a picture of an isolated Pete Hegseth who is hell-bent on continuing the Iran war, defending his job as defense secretary and desperately seeking President Donald Trump’s approval as he prepares for a potential presidential run.

“He’s a cross between a carnival barker and a personal trainer,” said John Ullyot, a former senior adviser to Hegseth and chief Pentagon spokesperson, to the outlet. Ullyot, whose new book is titled “The President Deserves Better: Leadership and Accountability to Keep America Great,” has called for Hegseth to resign.

In the Vanity Fair piece, Trump administration officials reflected on Hegseth’s “paranoia” and behavior, which a senior official claims stems from “Signalgate,” the instance last year when defense officials included a journalist from The Atlantic in a group chat discussing attack plans on Houthi rebels in Yemen.

“Every problem he is having in one way or another goes back to Signalgate,” a senior official told Vanity Fair. “His extremely hostile relations with the press, his paranoia, his firing of certain people, denied promotions to generals. It was all around paranoia related to Signalgate.”

Hegseth has faced a share of the blame for Republicans’ widespread losses in the midterm elections earlier this month since he spearheaded the unpopular Iran war.

He also narrowly dodged an impeachment effort after the elections.

Publicly, Trump has so far stood beside Hegseth, but the president has a history of flipping. Trump also has a notable turnover rate in his administrations.

“They [The White House] will stand behind him [Hegseth] in the short term,” a senior administration official told Vanity Fair. “He is a cost. He’s constantly requiring people to spend political capital on him. The White House is constantly having to come in and save him. The question is, at what point is it too much of a cost to the president?”

Hegseth will likely face another impeachment effort next year when the Democrats regain control of Congress.

Outside of the Iran war, his tenure is also plagued by his controversial decision to strike boats accused of carrying drugs — strikes that have killed at least 240 people. There are also allegations he was abusive to his second wife, which he denies.

The impeachment effort could also lead to noncongressional civil or criminal actions, even if he isn’t removed from office by a vote, Mother Jones reported Friday. Congress could also reduce Defense Department funding as a consequence, Mother Jones also noted.

The Department of Defense did not immediately respond to HuffPost’s request for comment.
